title: Scalable Lindblad Noise Learning via Stochastic Tensor-Network Simulation
authors: Alejandro R. Ramos Ramos, Maximilian Fröhlich, Aaron Sander, Robert Wille, Martin Eigel, Michael Hintermüller, Patrick Gelß, Sebastian Pokutta
abstract: Learning dissipation rates in large-scale open quantum systems is a major obstacle for near-term quantum technologies, as existing Lindblad estimation methods are typically limited to small system sizes due to the computational complexity of repeatedly solving the Lindblad equation during optimization. Here, we propose a scalable noise-learning framework for Lindblad dissipation rates that combines a stochastic simulation method, the Tensor Jump Method (TJM), with gradient-free optimization of a least-squares cost-function defined on time series of local-observable expectation values. We demonstrate the approach on two noise models in the Ising model: a site-resolved (local) model, in which independent dissipation rates are learned for each site up to $N_{\mathrm{site}}=16$, and a spatially homogeneous (global) model with only seven parameters, scaled to $N_{\mathrm{site}}=160$ sites.We complement these numerical results with a series of exact, provable guarantees: the Frobenius variance of the TJM density-matrix estimator is shown to equal $(1-\mathrm{Tr}[ρ^2])/N_{\mathrm{traj}}$, an exact purity-based characterization of the stochastic estimation error; the corresponding purity evolution is proven to be monotonically non-increasing for Hermitian jump operators; and, under a finite covariance distance assumption, the standard deviation of the cost-function is shown to decrease with system size, so that fewer trajectories are needed to reach a fixed target accuracy as the system grows. Together, this combination of scalable numerics and rigorous theoretical guarantees positions TJM-based noise learning as a practical foundation for characterizing dissipation in large quantum devices and for guiding future work on error mitigation and quantum error correction.
summary: This paper introduces a scalable framework to learn unknown dissipation rates in large open quantum systems by combining the Tensor Jump Method (TJM) with gradient-free optimization. By minimizing a cost function based on local observable measurements, the authors overcome the computational limitations of previous methods. The work is significant for its combination of scalable numerics and rigorous theoretical guarantees on estimation accuracy.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a scalable method to estimate dissipation rates (Lindblad noise) in large open quantum systems, as traditional methods fail due to the computational cost of solving the Lindblad equation repeatedly.
main_result: The authors propose a framework combining the Tensor Jump Method (TJM) with gradient-free optimization, demonstrating scalability to hundreds of sites while providing rigorous theoretical guarantees on the estimation error.
method: The approach uses TJM for stochastic simulation of open quantum dynamics, minimizing a least-squares cost-function defined on time series of local observable expectation values using optimization algorithms like CMA-ES or Bayesian Optimization.
model_or_system: The study uses the Ising model as a testbed, governed by the Lindblad master equation, incorporating both local and spatially correlated dissipation terms. The dynamics are simulated using tensor-network techniques (TJM).

main_assumptions: The theoretical error analysis assumes a finite covariance distance, and the optimization relies on the cost-function being differentiable or amenable to gradient-free search.
figures_summary: Figures compare optimization convergence (BO vs. CMA-ES) across various system sizes, show the evolution of global dissipation rates, and compare optimized vs. reference observable trajectories.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem and the TJM framework, then details the optimization setup using the Ising model, followed by rigorous theoretical analysis of the estimator variance and purity evolution, and concludes with numerical demonstrations of scalability.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical bottleneck in simulating realistic quantum devices by providing a scalable, statistically rigorous method for characterizing environmental coupling, which is crucial for error mitigation and quantum control.
